utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, all. Mr. Black, I guess you are still busy. We were talking yesterday before we broke off, if I can just -- there was an issue we were talking about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: At the very end, Your Honour, I believe we were talking about the idea that the barricades were spontaneous and whether they were everywhere, and Your Honour indicated that you would like to start up there again. I don't know if you have more questions on that topic this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, just maybe to reiterate the question that I put to the witness yesterday to say that at the end of the day yesterday I picked up that you are now saying that the barricades were between two villages. Previously you had said they were all over, and that because they were all over, they were spontaneous. I just want to get what actually your position is. Were they between two villages or were they all over? And whether they were all over or between two villages, how does that make them spontaneous necessarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's possible that there's an interpreting mistake. I thought, actually, that the barricades were on the inside and towards the outside. So somewhere on the outlying areas but somewhere also within that area, between our municipalities and settlements. That's what I was talking about. If the barricades hadn't existed between the different places, then it could have been something that had been thought out in advance. If they are within the area that is ours, it makes no sense for them to be organised. They would be making problems for themselves in that way. This is what I meant when I was describing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What problems would they be making for themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There would be a problem in reaching the different places in the communication. I already mentioned the problem between Knin and Gracac. These municipalities border on one another. There were several barricades, so we had a problem, and they also had a problem in getting through. Knin, Gracac, Lapac, and the other municipalities also had a problem with passage and communications at that time. If we could see a map, perhaps I could point to some locations that could illustrate what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not absolutely necessary. Okay. Thank you very much. I'll leave the point at that point. Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Licina. I have some more questions for you today. And I'll start on the same topic.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Because, in fact, there was a Croat population in this area and the reason there were internal barricades also was to restrict the movement of the Croat population. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not right. There is no Croatian village between Knin and Gracac. So that is not correct. This is exactly what I was talking about. The barricades were around each village practically. That's what I'm saying. It had nothing to do whether the village was Serbian or Croatian. That's why I said that it would be good perhaps to look at the map so I could show you where all these barricades were. For example, between Knin and Gracac there are no Croatian villages, but there were barricades put up in that area between Knin and Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You say it had nothing to do with whether the village was Serbian or Croatian, but that's not right. There were no barricades around the Croatian villages, were there? Only around the Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which villages had barricades specifically. They were all over the place. Barricades were all over the place, but it had nothing to do with it whether a village was Serbian or Croatian. I am -- I disagree with you that the barricades were erected around Croatian village to protect themselves from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Barricades were erected all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: My point was not that barricades were erected around Croatian villages to protect from the Serbs. My point was that the Serbs were erecting barricades so they could keep control of who was moving in the territory, specifically Croat population as well as any Croatian movement from the rest of Croatia. That's why the barricades were erected; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not right. The Serbs, the Serb population, erected the barricades out of fear and for protection because they were afraid that there would be incursions into the village -- villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yesterday, we talked a little bit about these barricades and you said you'd had to go to Knin after the 17th of August. So you yourself saw several of these barricades. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th of August, as we know, was our referendum. So it's normal that there was movement between the municipalities, because the referendum was under way. So I was on the road and I did have the opportunity to see where the barricades were. I had to take detours. I had to take side roads because --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt but you answered that question just by saying yes. You don't need to repeat what you said yesterday or the day before. And I had asked you yesterday -- I realised last night that I asked you specifically about barricades on the 17th of August, 1990, and about whether you knew that police had manned these barricades, but now I'm asking you about after the 17th of August, 1990, when you saw barricades. You did see that there were police or reserve police manning those barricades; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall seeing police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You do remember seeing men in uniform; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All the people that I saw were people in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of the barricades on TV or did you only see the ones that you saw personally?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably saw that on television as well. I also saw some for myself, and that's what I'm talking about. That's where the civilian -- people in civilian clothing were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So none of the barricades you saw on TV or personally there were men in uniform manning those barricades?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see people in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I suppose you also didn't see people carrying automatic weapons. You only saw hunting rifles. Is that what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, hunting weapons, personal weapons. Actually, there was a large number of unarmed people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Another thing you said yesterday on this same general topic was that you thought that the Croatian operations would have prevented the Serbian referendum had the army - by which you meant the JNA - not reacted by having a plane of the JNA turn back a Croatian MUP helicopter that had set off in the direction of Benkovac. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You know that Borisav Jovic was the president of the Presidency of the SFRY at that time of -- of Yugoslavia in August of 1990; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And he is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Mr. Licina and Mr. Black, but I seem to be getting a feed from the B/C/S translation somewhere on the line. I don't know what the technical problem is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I hear it too, Your Honour. I think it may be that the witness's microphones are picking it up from his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, is the volume okay on your headphones? If it's too loud or too quiet, please tell us and we can adjust that.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's okay now. It's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And my next question, Mr. Licina, was just to confirm: Borisav Jovic was a Serb; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Borisav Jovic was a member of the Presidency of the SFRY from the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And Veljko Kadijevic, another Serb, he was the Serbian secretary for national defence and the head of the JNA Main Staff at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was the secretary of national defence of the federal state. He wasn't the Serbian secretary. He was the federal secretary for national defence in the federal government. So he was a federal minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction. And you know that Borisav Jovic published a book of sort of his diary, his memoirs from the war. Are you familiar with that book?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the book was published, yes, but I didn't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that -- in that book Jovic says that Kadijevic told him that JNA planes never took off on that day, around those days, and that the Croatian helicopters were ordered back because they basically deviated from their approved course. Do you accept that, what Jovic says that he heard from Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't confirm that. I haven't read the book. This is something that Borisav Jovic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, if that's true, if what he says is true, then your explanation for why the Croatians were unable to stop the referendum because of this incident with the helicopter, well, that's just not accurate, is it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that I heard about the helicopter that was turned back. I cannot comment on a statement by Borisav Jovic. This is something that he said. You have to ask him about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to move to a different topic now, and it's also one we discussed yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, does the witness accept that it's true or not true? I'm not quite certain what to make of that answer. I thought that was the gist of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll put it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, it wasn't clear from your response: Do you accept or do you not accept that the JNA planes never took off and that the Croatian helicopters turned back for other reasons?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: I did have such information. The statement by Borisav Jovic is his statement. I cannot confirm it or deny it. I don't know what was happening at the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So your answer essentially is you don't -- you don't know whether that's true or not.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know what was happening at the Presidency and what the relations were between Borisav Jovic and Veljko Kadijevic, what their mutual orders were. I mean, I had no access to such information. I'm only talking about things that I know or that I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we interrupt you, Mr. Licina. Excuse me, Mr. Black. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor is answering instead of the witness. The witness said, "I heard that planes intercepted a helicopter. As to what Mr. Jovic said and what was happening at the Presidency is something that I don't know." And the Prosecutor is turning this answer by the witness into an alleged answer or response the witness that, according to the witness, he doesn't know what was going on. It's the wrong presentation of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes -- I hear what you said, Mr. Milovancevic, but I'm not quite sure I understand what your complaint is, because the witness clearly now says for the first time, which he didn't say yesterday, that his allegation about a JNA plane turning a Croat MUP helicopter is hearsay. Equally what he now hears about what Borisav said in his book is equally hearsay. He's prepared to accept the hearsay he heard. He's not prepared to comment on the hearsay he hears on the book. I'm not quite sure what actually your complaint is, and I thought this is the root that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness is explaining precisely that he doesn't know whether what Mr. Jovic is saying is hearsay. He said, "I heard that this was said. As to what Mr. Jovic himself said, I don't know because I wasn't at the Presidency." So the Prosecutor cannot derive from that something that the witness didn't actually say. In order to understand this situation, it's important what the Prosecutor is telling the witness in the question, that the helicopters of the Croatian MUP were turned back. How can the helicopters that were moving along the corridor be turned back? The only way -- they're not going to receive a note telling them to go back. The only way is for them to be intercepted and to be told to go back because they are in a space where they are not supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe you understand, Mr. Black. Would you like to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'll try, Your Honour. For one thing, I assume that those helicopters, like the other ones I'm familiar with, have radios. It's not necessary to pass notes to inform them that they need to come back to where they took off from. But the main point is he objects to me -- I think the objection is to me asking the witness, "So then you're saying you don't know," and that's exactly what the witness said. He said he doesn't know whether it's true or not, and that's also what Defence counsel said is that the witness said he doesn't know. I don't see anything objectionable about that question, and it was to clarify the answer to my original question, which was do you accept or don't you accept, which is the point of cross-examination, to ask him questions about whether he accepts these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought you wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Respond. Sorry, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In his testimony about this incident, the witness said, "I heard." He was very specific during the examination-in-chief and during the cross-examination. "I heard that this happened." At no point did he say, "I don't know if that happened or if it did not happen." He said, "I heard that the Croatian MUP helicopters took off." The Prosecutor confirms in his question that they did take off, and then the witness said, "And I heard that they were turned back by an intervention of the air force." All he said was what he had heard. Whether this happened or not is something that the Prosecutor can ask the witness and not just draw conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the conclusion that the Prosecutor is drawing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only the ones that suit them, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Identify the conclusion that you are saying -- you are objecting to that he has drawn, because then I must rule that conclusion out of order. But if you just --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I understand. In the examination-in-chief and during the cross-examination, the witness said those days, on the 17th of August, there was talk that the Croatian MUP helicopters had taken off and that they were turned back by the federal aviation of the JNA, and that is the course of the cross-examination. The assertion by the Prosecution that the witness stated that he does not know whether this happened is something that is just an opinion of the Prosecutor. It's not actually the words of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But now I'm not quite sure I know what you are trying say, Mr. Milovancevic. This witness, I think, just said now that he doesn't know. He has heard -- he had heard that the military intervened and turned the helicopter back. But he is here. We can find out. Did you hear or did you not hear about this incident of the helicopter being turned back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I heard about this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, can you explain to us from whom you heard that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was something that was reported in the media, also in conversations with other people from the party leadership. This was a very topical subject during those days. It was logical that we would discuss something like that. This is something that caused a lot of upset. Normally I don't know what happened in flight control or in the airspace, or what was happening in the aeroplane. Of course I couldn't know something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the specific question by the Judge is who told you that? You said you discussed it and it was topical. Who did you discuss it with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember specifically with whom, but I know that it was a topic that was discussed during those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not quite sure I understand --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- the Defence's objection. I'm not able to rule because I'm not quite sure what conclusion it is that the Prosecution is alleged to have come to. Maybe I just did not understand the proceedings at this stage. I'll have to listen again. May you proceed, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, you were just asked by His Honour Judge Hoepfel about how you -- who you heard this information from, and in fact you obtained this information much in the same way that you obtained a lot of the information that you've given here, which is that you either saw it on the news or you heard it from other people in the party or other people in your circle, social and political circle; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the only way, at the time, to get such information. I don't see any other way of getting information like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And -- and for both this fact and some others you didn't have first-hand, personal -- you're not saying that you saw this or you had first-hand information. You're just saying what you heard from other people and from the media; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First-hand information is something that only the pilot himself or flight control would have. So it's logical that the information I would have would be hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. But you agree with me, don't you, that Jovic and Kadijevic are more likely to know what was going on there than you did. They were likely to have more information about this incident than you had; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's up to them. It's their statement. I don't know what they knew and what they stated, or whether it's true what is said in the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I refrained from intervening, but what my learned friend the Prosecutor is doing now is improper. In its to date work, the Prosecution mentioned -- I'm just speaking at the top of my head now, but 100 -- page 188, and the title is the 17th of August, 1990. This is from Mr. Jovic's book. The Prosecution presented quotes from Mr. Jovic's book during these proceedings where Mr. Jovic cites a complaint by Croatian president Mr. Tudjman that two planes intercepted Croatian helicopters, and he considered that to be an attack on Croatia. And then in text after that, it is stated what the Prosecutor is presenting to the witness now. Perhaps my learned friend can show the witness the relevant part from the book, lay the grounds for that question, and then he can put the question to the witness. I cannot conduct the cross-examination myself. The Prosecutor needs to check his information. If he's referring to a book that has already been used in these proceedings, then he needs to present that evidence in the proper way. Right now I don't believe that he's doing that. The gist of my objection is that the Croatian president, Tudjman, asserted that JNA planes intercepted Croatian helicopters, and that is the reason why Mr. Jovic commented that incident in Croatian airspace at that time. My learned friend from the Prosecution is now trying to question the witness about how Mr. Jovic and Mr. Kadijevic are characterising that incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, just without giving me all this history, can you just tell me what your objection is in one sentence. I'd like to be able to say to Mr. Black what your objection is. I still don't understand. What is your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend from the Prosecution is not showing the relevant text from the book to the witness, and he is representing the -- what is written in the book incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is much clearer than that whole long story that you told me that I didn't understand. Mr. Black --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- would you like to respond to that objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I would like to respond to that, Your Honour. It seems to me that if Mr. Milovancevic wants to look at another portion of the book, he can do that on re-examination, but he has accepted that I correctly characterised the part of the book that says exactly what I've just been discussing, which is at page 160 in English, 178 in B/C/S. This is Exhibit 476 in evidence. The English ERN is 03022976. In B/C/S it's 01157839. That's the basis for my line of cross-examination. If he wants to look at other parts of the book, then I think he should do that in re-examination but otherwise I don't -- I don't see anything objectionable in my line of questioning, Your Honour. I hope I've understood the objection correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As I understand --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. As I understand Mr. Milovancevic, he would like you to show the witness the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Very well. I'm happy to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could we see Exhibit 476, please, on the screen in e-court. And again, if it's helpful, the passage I'm interested in is found on page 160 of the English, 178 of the B/C/S, and that's the part -- the numbers at the bottom of these photocopied pages. If it's of assistance, the English ERN is 03022976, and the B/C/S is 01157839. It may take a second to find this, Your Honours, because the -- because these are excerpts of the book the numbering -- the e-court numbering is slightly different, so I think it will take them a second to find the correct pages. If we could scroll down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I don't read B/C/S, but, Mr. Licina, maybe you could help us. Do you see on there the paragraph that begins, "Just as Pera Gracanin is leaving, Tudjman calls me up." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This microphone doesn't switch on when I press it. Okay. It's on now. Thank you. Are we going to see the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I hope -- I think the Court officer is working on it, and the usher are working on it right now, Your Honour. I think we have it now. Are you able to see it, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And perhaps I'll try to read out this entire passage to make sure that I'm capturing everything Mr. Milovancevic has also referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please follow along, Mr. Licina. "Just as --" And these are the words of Borisav Jovic: "Just as Pera Gracanin is leaving, Tudjman calls me up. Very upset. 'I beg of you, this is impermissible, we are the democratically elected government or are we not? We're not being allowed to exercise our legitimate authorities ...!' "'What's wrong?' I ask him." I won't give the quotes any more. "Some MiG fighters intercepted two of our helicopters and forced them to turn back and land --" this is Tudjman talking now -- "tanks are moving toward Croatia from Slovenia ... This is a scenario drawn up in Belgrade for overthrowing the legal Croatian government ..." And then Jovic comments on that. He says: "I barely got him to shut up. It is good that he's afraid. I promised him that I would look into the matter and get back to him." And here's the part that I was focussed on: "A conversation with Veljko Kadijevic revealed that almost none of this is true. The MiGs did not take off, the helicopters were returned by telecommand because they had deviated from the approved course ..." That's what it says there in Mr. Jovic's diary, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe it would help just to complete that sentence, to read that sentence to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That last sentence continues, after a semicolon: "... the reports of tanks from Slovenia are completely false." Should I continue with the paragraph or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I've read that out correctly; isn't that right, Mr. Licina? That's what Borisav Jovic says about this incident, this alleged incident.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic states here that he had been called by Mr. Tudjman, and such reports were circulating on Croatian TV anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Focus on my question. What I read out is what appears here in the book, in the B/C/S version. That's correct; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The translation may be slightly different, but that's what it says there. And you -- you must accept, don't you, that Jovic and Kadijevic were in a better position to know about this than you were?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but Tudjman seems to be saying here the same thing that I said. I don't know who is telling the truth here, but that's the information circulated by Croatian media at the time, and we were only able to follow the electronic media of Croatia, and that was the kind of report we were getting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any more questions on this particular topic. Unless you do, I'll move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: We're done with that document on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, now let me go back to another topic we talked about yesterday and ask you a quick question on this. This is again on constituent nation versus minority. You remember our discussion about this. And you remember saying - correct me if I'm wrong - but that the -- as a nation the Serbs essentially had a veto on the right of Croatia to secede. They had a voice. They could stop that process. Is that what you were saying yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not opposed in principle to giving the Prosecutor the right to interpret statements made by the witness, but what he just said is totally contrary to what the witness had stated. The witness never said that. I'm not going to say what the witness actually said, but only to avoid making suggestions or suggestive interpretations before the witness. What the witness talked about was the right to self-determination and the right to decision-making. He didn't talk about secession at all. He didn't talk about any unilateral acts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I agree with you that if Mr. Black is going to interpret the witness, he must correct -- he must interpret him correctly. But let's read what he asked. "Mr. Licina, now let me go back to another topic we talked about yesterday and ask you a quick question on this. This is again on constituent nation versus minority. You remember our discussion about this. And you remember saying - correct me if I'm wrong -" He's saying -- he's admitting that he made a mistake and he's asking to be corrected. So it's open to the witness to correct him, and I think -- let's listen to what the question is saying before we stand up to object. Now, Mr. Licina, if the question put to you by Mr. Black was wrong, please correct it and answer it. By "wrong" I mean if it misquoted what you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the question was what I considered under the term "constituent nation"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question was: Is it not so that the Serbs had a right of veto in the event Croatia wanted to secede? That -- I'm paraphrasing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not correct. Serbs had a right, as a constituent nation, to self-determination. A nation had a right to self-determination. That is, constituent nations had that right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I -- let me understand you. I understand the concept of nation. I'm not sure that I understand it the way you put it, but let -- I'm talking now about -- was it called a republic or was it called a province? Croatia as a province of Yugoslavia, or as a republic, a constituent Republic of Yugoslavia. If that republic wants to secede, would any of the constituent nations constituting that republic have a right of veto?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, sovereignty was not vested in republics but in constituent nations. That was written into the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I can clarify. I'll go straight to the transcript on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, yesterday I in fact asked you about something that you'd said before, and this is on page 50 of yesterday's transcript, and I asked you about something you said actually on page 72 of Monday's transcript, and this was about constituent nation versus minorities and the consequence of making the Serbs a minority rather than a constituent nation. And you said: "Had they been a minority, then the situation would have been different. They would have not had all the rights and there could have been a secession without approval of the Serbs. However, if Serbs are a constituent nation, then their consent is required for secession because a nation comes before a republic. That is the essence of that." You remember saying that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's completely in keeping with what I've just said. It is nations that are constituent, not republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And I want to focus on this one sentence that you say here: "If Serbs are a constituent nation, then their consent is required for secession." That's your position, right; that the Serbs have to consent or Croatia can't secede. That's what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was trying to say something else. Hypothetically, if both nations within Croatia agreed to go forward with secession, that was their right. But it was also the individual right of each of those nations to decide in what kind of state they wanted to live without prejudicing the rights of the other nation. We did not try to prejudice the Croats' right to self-determination. We just insisted on our own right to self-determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you're saying that Croatia had the right to secede. That's what you've just said. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not say that. I said the Croatian people had that right, but not Croatia as a republic, because Croatia was a republic of two nations. And that was the kind of issue that required the -- the agreement of both nations. If -- that such an agreement was impossible, then the republic had better change.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you or are you not saying that the Serb Nation had to approve for Croatia to secede? You've given both answers, but which is your position?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian people did not question the Croatians' right to self-determination. They just wanted the same right for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. I'm talking about the Croatian republic, not the Croat people or Croatian people. I'm talking about the Croatian republic. Did the Serb nation have the right to veto or give consent to Croatian secession from Yugoslavia? That's my question. What's your position on that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian republic was the state of the Croatian people and the Serbian people in Croatia. Sovereignty was vested in nations, not in republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Would you please answer my question. Could Croatia secede without Serbian approval? Without the approval of the Serb people in Croatia? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I gave you a very clear answer. I don't know what remains unclear to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just answer it, if you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, excuse me. May I intervene? This is a rather complex constitutional matter but it's not beyond understanding. If the Prosecutor is asking the witness what kind of right we are talking about, it's the right of nations to self-determination, then it would be logical for him to quote the specific constitutional provision. I'm trying to say one thing, Your Honour. The question, the way it was put, is a trap. The constitution of Yugoslavia envisaged the right to self-determination for every nation, and that's what the witness is talking about. However, it was the constitution of Yugoslavia, not the constitution of Croatia. Croatia was supposed to observe the constitution of Yugoslavia. There was a procedure for self-determination and that procedure was not observed. The way it was put, the question leads to a wrong answer because it is not in line with the existing constitutional arrangement, and the Prosecutor is making the witness give answers that are not understandable to the Trial Chamber. In fact, I'm trying to point out a problem. This is not a word game. This is not a matter in which one can answer yes or no. If one is seeking a yes or no answer, then one must proceed from constitutional provisions. Mr. Licina is not a lawyer, and he's not a constitutional expert, but his opinion on these matters is completely irrelevant, legally speaking. Mr. Licina is being asked to talk about constitutional matters and legal matters that he did not study. They were not included in his training. What is being sought from him, in fact, is a political position, and he is giving it. And Mr. Licina is, anyway, quoting the constitution correctly. But the Prosecutor is not showing any respect for the supreme legal act of a country when he's putting his question. He's totally misleading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think you must stop now. Mr. Milovancevic, thank you for your long story, but I just want to say to you when you do object, I would like you to please object appropriately. There is -- all the allegations you are making here are not correct. Mr. Black quoted from the transcript of yesterday what the witness said. We are not a constitutional law class here. We are just listening to evidence. That's all. And what the question -- what question is being put to this witness emanates from what this witness said himself yesterday. It has nothing to do with constitutional law. It has nothing to do with the constitution of the federation of SFRY or the constitution, if any, of Croatia. It's just got to do with the testimony of this witness that he made yesterday. Now -- and to suggest that the witness is being trapped or being asked constitutional questions is just not correct. He's being asked, "You said yesterday that Croatia cannot secede without the consent of the Serbian people in Croatia," and he just wants to establish that's his position. That's what he said yesterday. It was quoted. Unless you say he misquoted, I'm sorry, I cannot even -- I don't even want to hear his response. Do you have anything to say? And briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the reason for my intervention was the fact that, during examination-in-chief, the Defence asked this witness what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we are going to what this witness said yesterday that was quoted by Mr. Black. Is it wrong? If it is wrong, fine. Then Mr. Black must apologise and we'll censure him if he's misquoting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Black sought an answer and got it. Today, the witness repeated the answers he gave yesterday and the day before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What answer did he seek and what answer did he get? What is the question and what was the answer? And where is the answer on the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was about the status of constituent nation, and the witness repeated his answer that sovereignty in Yugoslavia was vested in nations and not in federal units, that is, republics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that's not Mr. Black's question. Mr. Black's question is: "You said yesterday that the -- Croatia could not secede without the consent of the people of Serb ethnicity who live in Croatia. Is that still your position?" That is the question. Having quoted what he said yesterday, he's saying, "Is that still your stand?" That's all the question there is. It's not a constitutional law question. It is not what you are saying he asked. Unless I'm misinterpreting your question. Is that question unfair? "Is it still your stand that Croatia could not secede unless the Serb people in Croatia consented?" That's the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness answered that question, and the Prosecutor is asking him the same question for the fifth time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was his answer, and where were the first four times? The question is, "Is that still your stand?" Because he has given two versions now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Prosecutor is questioning this witness concerning an issue of the constitution that the witness had referred to before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've just told you what the question was, and I'm asking you what was the answer by the witness to that question, "Is it still your stand?" Now, you're going back to analysing the Prosecutor's questions. I've told you the Prosecutor's question had nothing to do with constitutional law. It had to do with this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Prosecutor insists on the witness's opinion, then let the witness say it for the fifth time, but it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the essence of my objection, Your Honour, the essence of my objection is this: The Prosecutor is commenting upon the issue of the constituent character of a nation, and the witness is giving him an answer in keeping with the then existing constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Prosecutor is not commenting. The Prosecutor is asking a question. He's not commenting upon any issue. He's asking a question. "Is it still your stand that Croat Serbs must consent before Croatia can secede?" That's the question. That's not a comment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I understood you, and I agree, and I think the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please answer the question, sir. If you want to be reminded the question, you will be reminded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the Serbs were one of the two constituent peoples or nations, their consent was necessary for Croatia's secession. In other words, without Serbs, Croatia could not go forward with its secession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you happy with the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I can go from here, Your Honour. Thank you. But I would just say, Your Honour, before I continue with the questions, that it's very difficult for me to respond to any objection, which I'm not doing now, when they're constantly shifting objections. And also I object to Defence counsel testifying when the witness either can't or refuses to give answers. It's not proper for Defence counsel to step in and give what he wants the answer to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear what you say, and that's why I tried to say to Mr. Milovancevic we are not in a constitutional law class here and he must not turn the question into what he thinks it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I would say, as I continue, that this witness did testify about a number of constitutional-type issues and that's exactly why I'm going into this on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, you've now just said that without Serbs Croatia could not go forward with its secession, and that's the same as saying that Serbs have the power to essentially veto the secession of the Croatian republic; right? That's what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the power. It's just a Serbian right within Croatia, the right of Serbs as one of the two constituent nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You say it's the right but not a power, and you say that because in fact there was no provision of the 1974 Croatian or Yugoslav constitution that gave a mechanism for the Serbs to prevent this kind of secession. There was no mechanism by which the Serbs could exercise this right, was there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are not correct on that. There was a mechanism and there was a commission called the Commission on the Equality of Nations and Minorities, or ethnicities, within Croatia, and that commission had to deliberate on all issues that touched upon the equality among nations and ethnicities, and all its decisions had to be taken by consensus. The new Croatian authorities failed to elect that commission in due time, and in that way they failed to observe the rules. They went around certain regulations and this rule was violated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And your position is that this commission had the final say about even issues like secession. This commission had to approve this -- you know, commission with both ethnicities had to approve or Croatian could not secede. That's your position?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since the Croatian parliament did not have the Chamber of Nations, it was precisely this commission that was authorised to deal with these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was this commission -- does this appear in the constitution? Was this something that was required by the constitution or this was just part of the internal workings of the Croatian parliament?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is regulated by legislation. I'm not sure. I'm not a lawyer, but I think that it was regulated by legislation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But you don't really know because you're not a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not a lawyer. But since I was a deputy in the Croatian parliament, I know that this commission did not exist up until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Had the commission existed before? And, if so, when did it stop existing?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commission existed up until 1990, up until those elections. In accordance with the rules of Procedure of the parliament, it was supposed to be established at the constituent session. The Croatian parliament was constituted on the 30th or 31st of May, 1990, which is when all boards and commissions of the parliament were established. However, this particular commission was not established, and it was not until mid-December of 1990 that it was finally established.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry -- now, to make sure I'm understanding you correctly, you're now saying that it's this commission, the failure to form this commission is what meant that the Serbs couldn't exercise their veto over the secession of the Croatian republic. That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Black, this was not just an ordinary failure. If all commissions and boards of the parliament establish, except for this one, this one which is extremely important, which plays a key role in these issues, then I don't think this is just a mere failure or omission. I think that this speaks of a clear intent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's your point of view both personal and political; right? That is your point of view, your opinion.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my position, and that was the position of all Serbs, the majority of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And your position and the position of all Serbs was, therefore, that a numerical minority of Serbs acting through this commission should have been able to stop the efforts of the entire Croatian republic to secede from Yugoslavia. That was your right and that's the way it should have been. That's what you insisted on.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't perceive Serbs as a numerical minority. I perceive Serbs in Croatia as one of two constituent nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, we've been through that, and I think we're going to move on to the next -- the next topic. You remember yesterday when we talked about the Serb Assembly in Srb on the 25th of July, 1990, and you told us - and I can find the transcript if I get this wrong, so let me know - you told us that was not about independence. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb Assembly in Srb on the 25th of July, 1990, was the largest political gatherings of Serbs up until that time. It had nothing to do with independence. It was about the -- adopting the declaration on sovereignty and autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a video clip, and it's from Exhibit 497, but we'll have to show it on the Sanction, of course, because it's a video. If we could please switch to Sanction. And if Ms. Walpita could broadcast Sanction. Okay. If we could play that first clip from V000-6690, please. Just watch this, Mr. Licina. I think the e-court button should still work for this. We're hoping that the technical issues from yesterday have been solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think that was sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, Mr. Martic is exactly right, isn't he? That was the first attempt of creating a self-reliant and independent state.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. President Martic just gave his interpretation here. He speaks of some kind of a continuity. He speaks about this being some kind of a beginning. However, we cannot say that this was the beginning of a creation of a state. You can't find this in any of the documents. Look at the declaration which was adopted at this Assembly. No independence whatsoever is mentioned there, no secession.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, put aside the issue of what's in the documents. What about reality? The reality of the fact is exactly as Mr. Martic says, that this was the first attempt of creating a self-reliant and independent state. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Black, that's not true. At the Assembly in Srb, Serbian National Council was founded and the declaration on sovereignty and autonomy of Serbian people was adopted. I don't see how this has anything to do with independence or secession. Everything that happened later was a product of the conduct of the Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe we have about three minutes left but I'm about to go into a larger topic. It might be a convenient time to break right now, if that's acceptable to Your Honours. We can even start five minutes earlier. Am I right about the time? We usually stop at 10.15, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are right about the time; we usually stop at 10.15. We will take those extra minutes as a bonus. So we'll take a break and come back at quarter to. Thank you, Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, yesterday we talked a little bit about the HDZ, which was a Croat party in Croatia, as you said. Now I'd like to ask you some questions about the SDS, your own party. Jovan Raskovic was the founder of the SDS in Krajina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovan Raskovic was the president of the Serbian Democratic Party and one of the founders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And he was the president essentially from the beginning, from the founding of the party; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Am I correct that he was -- he was relatively moderate in his views? He wasn't seen at the time as particularly extreme?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In fact, he was actually kind of ousted from the SDS leadership around July of 1990 or thereafter because he spoke with Tudjman, and that was the time the SDS was becoming more radical; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That didn't happen in July of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When did that happen, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovan Raskovic was never ousted from the SDS. He led it throughout the time. It was just that Milan Babic split with some of the members and created a new wing of the party. I think it was in late 1991 or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me focus for the time being on Raskovic, and I'm just going to ask -- well, it's true that Jovan Raskovic used pretty extreme language at times in 1990 and 1991. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true, no. To my knowledge, Jovan Raskovic never used any radical or extreme language. He was an academician and a physician, a psychiatrist, and he was seen as a representative of the people. That's how we perceived him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black, perhaps between you and the witness might understand what extreme language means. That's more of an evaluative term and what is extreme to you may not necessarily be extreme to me. Is it possible for you to say exactly what it is that he said, and let's find out and maybe compare it to what he said earlier that you regard as mild so that the Chamber can see what is meant by extreme here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. You anticipated my next move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could please see on the e-court a document bearing the ERN 02927453 to 7457. The English translation is those same numbers preceded by the letters ET.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, as we're waiting for this to come up on the screens in front of us, you're aware that Jovan Raskovic published --

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It came up, but in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Hopefully we can rectify that. I don't have it at all on my monitor, actually, in any language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence doesn't have it either.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it now in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you check that the Defence has it too?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: There is a possibility that we could still be on Sanction as far as the audiovisual goes. No, apparent -- here we go. We have it all sorted out. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the second page there on the B/C/S version. This is still the first page of the English translation. These are -- Mr. Licina, these are a number of excerpted pages from a book published by Jovan Raskovic in 1990 called "Crazy Land." Have you heard of this book before?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me read out to you -- if we could scroll down slightly on the page in B/C/S. Just follow along. I'm going to read a selection from Mr. Raskovic's book. It says: "The Ustasha movement is also a rational delirium. Already in 1940, when Ustashas were planning the destruction of the Serbs, they made exact geography of all the pits on the territory of the NDH," which refers to the Independent State of Croatia. "Not only did they do this but they also calculated the dimensions of the pits and determined how many bodies of children and women would fit in each pit. In that way they knew exactly what and how much they could 'do.' The delirium of the slaughter and genocide that took place in 1941 against the Serb people was a rational delirium, and that is why it had such an epochally high 'score.'" The next paragraph, I'll read that out as well. It says: "The delirium of the Mass Movement in Croatia in the seventies had rational programs but it was stopped on the political level. If it had not been stopped on that level, that delirium could have probably been realised, and it would have become a murderous delirium. It would have been murderous because it was anti-Serb, genocidal - and it was stopped in the phase of the political genocide against the Serbs. But, there is a short way between the political and the real genocide." Now, Mr. Licina, looking back, do you recognise that publishing works like this in 1990 was likely to have an adverse effect on Croat-Serb relations?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This book, this text was published by Jovan Raskovic not -- in his capacity not only of a politician but also a psychiatrist. And as far as I can tell, this represents a kind of a professional text. I don't see any problem in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Jovan Raskovic was, as you said, the president of the SDS and one of its founders and really the leader of the SDS. You accept that this book was widely read at the time, in 1990 and thereafter, don't you? This was an important statement.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovan Raskovic is an academician. He was a psychiatrist, a scholar, and this book had more of a scholarly dimension than a populist one. It was widely read in scholarly circles but not by general public. These are not topics generally discussed by ordinary people. The majority of them don't even understand half of these terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, the majority of the people came to understand, if they didn't understand before, the term "Ustasha" and the term "genocide," didn't they? Because these were terms that the SDS leadership, including Mr. Raskovic, pounded into them in 1990 and 1991, and thereafter as well.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ustashas and genocide is something that happened. These are not invented things. So I don't see a problem there. To this day we have painful memories of that. Something resembling that surfaced again, and I don't see what is problematic about mentioning it again. It was logical to mention it. And this is a scholarly text written by a professional within the professional domain. That was the content of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. A professional who was also the president of the SDS; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was president of the SDS, but he was also an academician and a psychiatrist, and that was the source of his income, not politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'd like to look at another -- another passage from this book. I'm just trying to find it for you in the B/C/S. He makes a reference to Kosovo, so if you see that there, please help me find it. It's a paragraph that starts: "You can't find many nations in the world except the Jews, Armenians and Gypsies ..." Are you able to see that on that page anywhere, Mr. Licina?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could we turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may be of assistance. It's page 208 in the B/C/S version. I don't know if this is what my learned friend had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. I'm extremely grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. And if we could scroll down to the bottom of that page. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, please follow along. It's actually a little further in that paragraph, and it starts there the first two words on the bottom of the page and then we will have to scroll up to the top. And it says: "Suffering of the Serbs was a rule of history. The only thing that has been happening to the Serbs from the battle of Kosovo until the present time was a huge suffering. Only God's justice saved the Serbs from annihilation and from complete disappearance of the Serb name. In every century hundreds of thousands or millions of the best among the Serbs dedicated to their faith and nation were paying their dedication with their lives. The Serb nation has been undergoing destruction for six centuries." Now, those were the views of the -- one of the founders and the president of the SDS. Do you share those views? Did you share them then, and do you share them now?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Both then and now I adhere to these views. The Serb people have been destroyed through the centuries, and it is normal for us to speak up about that. Can you imagine what would happen, how terrible it would be if the Jews were forbidden to speak of Holocaust?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. No one is suggesting you should have been forbidden to speak of it. You said -- actually, I don't see it in the transcript, but in fact you and other Serb leaders, especially in the SDS, you emphasised this suffering of the Serbs in order to galvanise the Serb people, to get their backing in your political moves, including seeking a separate Serb state; isn't that right? That was of the point of constantly these references to Serb suffering.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not the point. Any regular Serb will tell you the same thing that I am telling you. We have preserved our tradition, the tradition about the battle of Kosovo. It's a national myth on which the Serb nation was built. In our activities, at least in the beginning, in our political activities there was no mention of secession. All we wanted to do was to fight for the rights of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And let me focus still on these kind of statements. You as a Serb politician, you knew that by generating fear in the Serb population by references to genocide and Ustasha, and then also emphasising Serb suffering, you knew that this was a way that you could win the support of the Serb people. That's why these kind of things were referred to by Serb politicians. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You are not right. All we did was refer to Serb history. Unfortunately, Serbian history is what it is. It's bloody with a lot of casualties, and how could anybody have the right to deny us to talk about that? This is something that everyone talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be put in evidence, please; given a number and admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document will become Exhibit 874.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'd like now to show another clip. This clip is part of the video marked V000-5875. And we'll show this again on the Sanction. So if we could move to the Sanction system. Okay. Everything seems to be ready. Mr. Licina, this is from a documentary entitled "Neighbours," and as you'll see here, I believe in the first frame, this is footage from a rally on the 17th of August, 1990. And could we go ahead and see the clip now, please. Your Honour, it seems all we do is sort out problems with Sanction. If I could have a few seconds to try this again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think we've got it sorted out, Your Honours. If we could now watch the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, you would accept at least that there was extreme language, comments, remarks being made by SDS supporters, and in that case kind of encouraged by Jovan Raskovic; right? Or do you find that those chants by the crowd in the video were justified?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say "SDS supporters." What I see here are people who are chanting slogans, but I don't know if they are SDS supporters. I also see Jovan Raskovic, who is telling them not to ask him to give them weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What does he mean when he continues and says, "... but if you need weapons, you'll probably find someone who will give them to you"? What do you understand him to mean there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he meant. I am not about to guess what he meant to say by that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, just give me your opinion. In your opinion, was he discouraging those people?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is footage taken during one of the crises, and if I remember correctly, this is a propaganda film by the Croats, called "Neighbours," and what they did is take excerpts, and then by putting together certain excerpts out of context, a certain story was presented. This is typical propaganda material. So I really cannot comment about something that is -- well, this is really taken out of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Give me the context. Explain how it's justified when the crowd chants, "We will kill Tudjman. We will kill the Ustashas," and Jovan Raskovic says, "Well, don't ask weapons from me, but somebody else I'm sure can be found to give you weapons." Give me the context that justifies that.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a context because I am not able to hear the entire speech. So I cannot really comment on just a segment. It's just a sentence from a political speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, what -- this -- according to the documentary, this is a speech given on the 17th of August, 1990. Was there anything in the circumstances that you think justifies the chants of the crowd and Raskovic's interaction with them?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for mentioning that. If this was on the 17th of August, did it take place somewhere in Dalmatia, for example? If it was on the 17th of August, was this in Dalmatia? I think judging by the way the people there are speaking, this was then somewhere in Dalmatia, in the area of Benkovac during one of the major crises. I think we spoke about that period. It was a time of confiscation of weapons, takeover of police stations. It was a time of high tension and great fear amongst the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And this rally wasn't even that unusual in the kind of views being expressed by the crowd there at that time. That was not just limited to this rally but other rallies at that time. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was a rally that was like that. Rallies differed from one rally to another. You cannot say that every single rally was like this. This was a rally at a very stressful neuralgic time. Therefore it's one thing to take it out of context and to present that as the manner of the political activity of the SDS. After all, this is a meeting after the SDS elections, so there is no sense for the SDS to be promoting some sort of its own programme at rallies like that. This is probably just some kind of gathering after that. This is not a political rally as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, the SDS didn't cease to function as a political party after the elections. That can't be what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not what I'm saying. But this is not an election rally so that there would be something like the political programme being presented. This seems to me some sort of a protest at the time when there was a crisis, and it's quite a different tone that such a meeting would have compared to other political rallies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could this clip be admitted into, please, and given a number, Your Honour? It also does have a transcript which we'll put in e-court along with the clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The clip is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number and, if possible, can we also give an exhibit number to its transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think the practice with other clips is to have the same number and they'll both appear there, Your Honour. But however it is best for the court officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The court officer will know what to do.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit number 875.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, it wasn't just Jovan Raskovic who made these kind of statements. Other SDS leaders also -- well, in that case it was the crowd, but other SDS leaders used words like "Ustasha" and "genocide" and used that kind of language, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must object. The excerpt, we heard only one sentence by Mr. Raskovic: "Do not demand weapons from me. If they are needed, somebody will be found to give them to you." Mr. Raskovic did not mention Ustashas. The Prosecutor seems to be suggesting that Mr. Raskovic himself mentioned killings, Ustashas, and so on, but this is quite incorrect. He did not say anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If I could respond, Your Honour. What I said was -- I corrected myself. I said, oh, in that case it was the crowd, but other SDS leaders used words like "Ustasha" and "genocide," used that kind of language. So I absolutely accept that Mr. Raskovic did not use that language in the clip, but that wasn't my question, at least my intended question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But be that as it may, the Exhibit 874, doesn't it mention Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, it did, Your Honour, and that was the basis for me saying that was the crowd had mentioned "We will kill the Ustashas." That's what I was segueing from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: As well as the prior exhibit also referenced "Ustasha."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, are you happy with that correction?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, the question was - and I'll try to say it more clearly - and let me take someone specific. Milan Babic, who was a member of the SDS and the Serb leader in Krajina, he used words like "Ustasha" and "genocide" in his public statements, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he used those terms when he was making his appearance. He probably did. I don't know. But these terms "Ustasha" and so on were used. I don't see anything disputable about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you yourself used the term "Ustasha" in public addresses, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not use it in a public address. I used it in a specific case. If it referred to Ustashas, then I would speak or use the word "Ustashas." Just to remind you, Ustashas are a Croatian force during World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But you actually also used "Ustasha" to talk about Croatians or Croatian forces in the 1990s, didn't you? And you did so publicly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness said fascist forces in World War II.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I didn't use that term. I used the term "Ustashas" in a specific context. When Ustashas were discussed, that was the term I used. I mean, when that was the topic of a discussion, I had no choice but to use that term. What else could I do?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You're saying now that you only used the term "Ustasha" to talk about fascist Croatian government authority in World War II?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatian fascists. Croatian fascist forces in World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could we please see on e-court a document with ERN 02169807 to 9808. And we need to make sure we change back from Sanction to e-court. Thank you. And, Your Honours, this is a document that I do not believe we have an English translation for, so we'll just have to use the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those of us who are limited in language --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That includes me, Your Honour. What I planned to do was ask the witness to read out the particular passage and then the translation will tell us what it says. Could we please scroll down on the page. There, I think, is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, the -- look at that last paragraph that's visible there. I can even tell you -- could you please read out the last three sentences, or at least that third sentence from the end.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph again?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually, it just kind of moved. Before we get there, if we could scroll up a bit more -- sorry, scroll to the top for a second. I'll ask a question before we get to the specific quote. This is -- this is you addressing the first session of the RSK parliament in October of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If we could scroll back down. It's -- unfortunately, I can't even tell you what the first word -- right now it's the last paragraph that's visible there at the bottom of the screen. The last full paragraph. That one. If you could -- now it's sort of in the middle of the screen. You can probably see the word "Ustasha" in there a couple of times. Could you read out the sentence in which the word "Ustasha" appears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which one is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: He should know, Your Honour, not us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: We'd like to identify it as well, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Because I want to make sure I'm on the same paragraph that you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you find that sentence, Mr. Licina?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could you read it out and then afterwards I'll have you circle it so that we know which one you're going to. For the time being, please just read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like this: It's a document that is my speech at the Assembly in Beli Manastir in 1993, after the attack on the Medak pocket by Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you reading?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to read now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am reading now. I'm going to read now -- the whole paragraph, or that sentence, "As for ..."?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
