utterances.text: Just that one sentence, please. We'll start with the sentence and then if you feel it's necessary to read the paragraph for context, then you're more than welcome to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "As for the Ustashas who left at 6.00 and arrived at Sitnik at 8.00, the Ustashas were not stopped. They stopped by themselves. There is no need for anybody to grab a credit for stopping someone and in what way. No. They simply stopped."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. That's not a reference to World war II, is it? That's a reference to 1990s.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand whether the witness said yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we just didn't -- we didn't pick up your response, your answer to that question. This was not a reference to World War II, was it? It was a reference to the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This took place after the Croatian attack on the Medak pocket in 1993. It's the Assembly in Beli Manastir. That's what it says at the top of the page. It's the Beli Manastir Assembly following the Croatian attack on the Medak pocket when about 100 people were killed in the area of the Donji Lapac and Gracac municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And your references here to Ustasha do not refer to World War II, they refer to that that you've just described; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It refers to the same acts as the ones committed by the Ustashas in World War II. Four Serbian villages were completely ethnically cleansed, burned down. Everything was killed, including the -- the domestic animals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: See if you can answer my question. This is not a reference to World War II, is it? It's a reference to Croatians or Croatian forces in 1990s. In 1993, I think you said.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it refers to the Croatian forces in 1993 which did this. And the forces that did something like that I would call the same thing now, today. Somebody who committed such a bestial act is the same as the Ustashas in World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be admitted into evidence, please. And what I'll do is request -- oh, actually, would you like me to have the witness circle the sentence or is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: With the assistance of the court usher, Witness, we're just going to, just for the benefit of those of us who don't speak your language, if you could just use the pen that's given to you by the usher and just circle at least the paragraph where you've read from, that reference to Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And did -- correct me if I'm wrong, you've then circled -- is that the sentence where the reference is? I just want the record to be clear.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the sentence in which Ustashas are mentioned three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And since it's Cyrillic script, which is a little unfamiliar for us, could you circle the word "Ustasha" each of the three times it appears so that we can see how that looks in Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Licina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, then could this view please be made another exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It needs to be saved and then it becomes an electronic exhibit like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll do that. Shall we at some stage get a translation of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we'll request a translation and put that into e-court along with it as soon as we get it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May this document please be given an exhibit number. It is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this will become Exhibit number 876.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, just for my clarification is 876 the image or is that the full document? I didn't make it clear. There needs to be two different exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There's no way you can admit into evidence the quotation without the document, can you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The problem is, and I think it's just a technical one, is that in order for them to capture the fact that the witness has circled the sentence and the words, that image on our computer has to be saved and become an exhibit so we have that for the future. So that should be one exhibit, and then the entire document where the whole document shows up, that should be another exhibit, I think. If that's acceptable to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So what is it you want to be Exhibit 876, just this image and not the entire document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm in your hands whichever one is which. Whichever is simplest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're the dominus litis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Why don't the whole document be 876, and then this screen view can be the next exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The whole document, then make it 876, and the image on the screen, make it the next number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, so the marked document will become Exhibit number 877.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That page. Thank you very much. And then so that we can use this 876 immediately, Mr. Black, perhaps you then must move that the entire document be admitted into evidence as -- or has it been admitted? Okay. Fine. It has already been admitted. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, you just explained that you think that people who committed the kind of acts that you referred to, they also deserved to be called Ustashas; right? Is that -- am I understanding you correctly?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And in fact, that was sort of the practice among SDS officials and other Serb leaders, was if you felt it justified, you would use the word "Ustasha" for Croats or Croatians or the Croatian authorities in the 1990s even though that's obviously a different thing than the government from World War II; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. This is a speech from the Assembly session of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina in Beli Manastir, which was held after the Croatian attack on the Medak pocket. In that Croatian aggression, many of my friends were killed, acquaintances, and it's normal that the people who could do something like that I would call them Ustashas. How else could I call them; brothers, friends?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: My question is not just about that particular instance but in general in 1990, 1991, 1992, 1993, in that time, SDS leaders, SDS members, yourself included, used the word "Ustasha" whenever you felt it was justified. It didn't have to refer to World War II; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That's not right. In this case it's more than justified. I have very clearly answered how and why I happened to use that term, and once again I will call the people who committed that Ustashas here before this Tribunal. I have no other term to describe them, but I do not wish to generalise in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, the question is not in this case. This case has been dealt with, the case of your speech in 1993. The question is this term was used, generally speaking, among SDS members in reference to Croatian people. Is that so or is it not so? I think the question is simple enough to answer on a simple yes or no basis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give you a very simple answer: No, we did not use such terms. We used them only in such extreme cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Actually, if we could see another video clip now on the Sanction. This is from V000-3865.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And, Mr. Licina, this, I believe, is a speech given on the 25th of July, 1991, by Jovan Raskovic. So if we could broadcast the Sanction, and just watch on your screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, this is July, 1991, and Raskovic is essentially calling for violent resistance by Serbs against what he calls a genocidal Croatian state. Do you still deny that SDS leaders were using very provocative language?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do deny. We can see it clearly here. Jovan Raskovic says if two Ustashas show up, to take them to the pit and kill them there. Because such cases did happen in Second World War. People were tied up and two or three men would kill them while they were standing over pits. So he was just saying that they should not walk to their graves alone. They shouldn't walk to the pits on their own. I don't know what you mean by this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, this is just part and parcel of the Serb and the SDS propaganda that's trying to equate events in 1990s with World War II in order to cause fear in the Serb population, fear of Croats and Croatians. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is no propaganda. In World War II, a million Serbs lost their lives. In this war, almost a million Serbs were expulsed -- expelled. What is the difference? Croatia is an ethnically cleansed state. What were we supposed to do, throw flowers on them?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The clip is made an exhibit, admitted as an exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit number 878.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I'd just like us to look at one more document with regard to Mr. Raskovic. And let me see if I can find the ERN. This is something that had an ERN recently. I believe the ERN is 06030302. While we're waiting for that, Mr. Licina, you accept at least that the effect of this kind of language by the SDS and its leaders was to cause fear among the Serb population. You accept that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not he who caused fear among the Serb population. It was their experience. The Croatian policy during World War II was to convert one-third of the Serbs, to kill one-third of the Serbs, and to expel another third. 67.000 were killed in this war; around 10.000, according to our information, were converted only in the parish of Zagreb. So the principle is exactly the same. And many more were expelled. You seem to be saying that people were made afraid by this speech. They were not. They were made afraid by what was going on, by what was happening to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could scroll down on the page that you see in front of you have. This is -- that's perfect. That's a quote of Jovan Raskovic and was published on the 27th of January, 1992, in Vreme magazine. Do you see there it has Jovan Raskovic in sort of big letters on the right side of the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, this is another document that translation has been requested but we don't have it yet, so we'll have to ask the witness to assist us again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, if you find that -- that's plenty of focus there, I think. Could you read out what Jovan Raskovic says in this interview, please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovan Raskovic said in a Jutel programme, "I feel responsible because --"

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise. It's simply a technical thing. The interpreters are going to have to keep up with you as you read, so please try to make an effort and read slower than usual. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In a weekly television programme on Jutel television, Jovan Raskovic said: 'I feel responsible because I have made preparations for this war, although those were not military preparations that I made as somebody who sees war as a solution, but if the emotional fire had not been stoked among the Serbian people, even that would not have come to pass. In fact, my party and I personally just ignited the fuse of Serbdom but not only in Croatia.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think that's far enough. Even Jovan Raskovic recognised the impact of the kind of statements made by him and by the SDS on the Serb population. He recognised it. Do you still deny that it had that effect?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Jovan Raskovic stated this just before he died, and in some ways he must have been disappointed, I believe. When he says that his party ignited the fuse of Serbdom, I don't see what kind of problem you have with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm not saying I have a problem with it, but it's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbian Democratic Party ignited the fuse of Serbdom in the area of the former Republic of Croatia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be admitted into evidence as well, please, and we'll provide the translation as soon as we receive it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number and may a corresponding number be given to the translation as and when it is received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document will become Exhibit number 879.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, let me -- let me change topics a little bit now. Yesterday, kind of chronologically we'd gotten up to about August of 1990. I'm going to continue from there for the time being. On the 25th of August, 1990, I believe you testified on Monday that you attended a session of the Croatian parliament. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly on the 25th or on the 26th of August, but, yes, that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could please see on the e-court a document, it's a newspaper article, and it bears the ERN 02664600. If we could enlarge that a bit to focus in on the third column.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could enlarge a bit to focus on the third column, and maybe even a little bit more. If we could focus in. I do have an English translation but I want to make sure the witness has the ability to follow along. I think that's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a tiny bit more. Could you raise it a bit, please. Upwards. No, no, no. It's okay now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: As -- as depicted in this article, Mr. Licina, you attended this session in essence to explain why the other SDS parliamentarians did not attend. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: According to this article, a little ways into that first paragraph, it says -- and this is attributing words to you. It says that you said: "A Serbian populace in Croatia is a political population older than the Croatian political population. It's easy to find historical evidence about the existence of Serbian parties in Dalmatia while it was still under the strong arm of Venice. The same goes for Slavonia where there were also Serbian parties while it was under the rule of the Vienna crown." And then you say: "Croatian political population is formed slightly later in accordance with political projects by Starcevic." Now, that's a reference to the Ustasha leader Ante Starcevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not the Ustasha leader Ante Starcevic who is mentioned. It is Ante Starcevic, leader of the Croatian Party of Rights from the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So you're saying --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The 19th century. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what was -- how would you characterise the political viewpoint of that person, Ante Starcevic, then? Was he also a Croatian nationalist or a fascist leader even though he wasn't part of the Ustasha movement?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ustashas and fascism appeared actually 10 years later or so, but Ustashas drew a lot in terms of ideology from ideas of Ante Starcevic. I cannot say exactly -- it's exactly the same thing because they did not exist at the same time, but Ustashas did find inspiration in the Croatian Party of Rights. This requires a knowledge of history to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I think I understand your explanation. And my point really is that here on -- in August of 1990, you're insinuating that Croatian political identity essentially springs from fascism, or at the very least the ideas of Starcevic. Before that there really was no Croatian political identity. That's what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm just saying which of the two peoples in Croatia were older, politically speaking. It was the Serbs. Serbs had a state earlier, had one form of political entity in the Austro-Hungarian monarchy in which they were given a military krajina, that is a border area, before Croatia ever existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry to interrupt. We didn't need another history lesson about the Serb people. But you were basically saying that Croatian people, their political identity begins with Starcevic, with his ideas in the 19th century. That's what you were saying right there; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're talking about Croatian political organisation, then the answer is yes, it did begin with Starcevic in terms of defining the Croatian national platform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: A little further down in this article - we'll have to scroll down - you see another sort of heading there which I believe says "Night refuges a reminder of war." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And actually, that continues on to the next page in B/C/S, but this is a photocopy of the top part and the bottom part of a newspaper page. So if we could go to the next page in the e-court, please. Can we go -- there's only one page in -- perhaps we can -- I have a hard copy, if we can put it on -- give it to the witness. I'll read it out in English, but I just want to make sure the witness is able to see. Sorry for the delay, Your Honours. I just want to make sure he's able to follow along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What page are we supposed to be at?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This is -- on the English it's the bottom of page 1 of the translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And if you can find where I'm reading there, Mr. Licina, just please follow along. It says, and this is a reference to a gathering of signatures to expel some academy members, including --

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not hearing you so well any more. It may be something wrong with the headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for mentioning that. We'll try to resolve that right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As you resolve that, can you also point us, Mr. Black, to exactly where you are reading. I've got the bottom of page 1, and the last paragraph starts with: "This, Ratko Licina said, which is still happening to the Serbian people in Sibenik and in --"

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's exactly where I'm going to read from.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you hear me better now, Mr. Licina?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I start reading, let me just say, there's a reference here to gathering signatures for a petition to expel academy members, including Jovan Raskovic. Could you just explain in one or two sentences what that was all about? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. Signatures were being collected for Jovan Raskovic as president of the SDS; for Branko Popovic, general secretary; and Marko Dobrijevic, organisational secretary of the SDS. Those people were living in Sibenik, and signatures were collected for expulsion from Sibenik. And when you are expelling people from their birthplace, there's no other name for it than fascism, and that's why I called it fascism. It's linked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How can there be a petition for expulsion of someone from their town? Who is doing this petitioning? I don't understand. You'll have to explain to me what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the Croats from Sibenik and Sibenik area who organised this. The Croatian authorities in Sibenik. It was some sort of a petition. It was a horrible thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And so I understand it, they were basically collecting signatures saying that those people needed to leave the town that they lived in. Is that what you're saying? Sort of citizens collecting signatures; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Yes. Yes. It was horrible. I don't know how else -- what else to call it but fascism.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And in the last sentence of that paragraph, you say, don't you: "After 2.000 years, this is an act of genocide and a genocidal relapse of one policy." You actually equate this gathering of signatures -- you say that that's genocide, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- expelling, exiling people from a town is a form of genocide, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And this is just one example of something that the SDS did a lot in 1990, which was take some political move by the Croatian side and label that as genocide. That was something that the party did regularly; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. The party didn't do that on a regular basis. The party did that in cases when Croatian authorities made moves that deserved to be characterised in that way. Whenever Croatia made a move that was fascist and Ustasha in nature, we called it that. We just called a spade a spade. We did not use that term constantly. Regrettably, there was more than enough cause for using that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you don't see any difference between this kind of political move, reprehensible as it may have been, and genocide. You still to this day equate those things.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that move was fascist and genocidal. I believe it to this day, and I see no reason why I should not call things by their name. What do you mean? Do you mean that by calling it genocide I am making a graver violation than the people who originally made that step?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's not a question of comparing your violation with someone else. The point is, by calling this genocide, you and other Serb leaders were exaggerating the situation. You were trying to draw comparisons with World War II in an effort to create fear among the Serb population. That's what it was all about, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true, Mr. Black. I'm talking about a specific case, the expulsion of three men, and that was a fascist move, and I'm prepared to say it in these words to this day. I don't see what the problem is. What would you call it? Was it a tourist package tour for them?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be admitted into evidence, please? And we're also done with the ELMO. I know it's difficult for the witness to see me the way the ELMO is now, so if we could lower it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 880.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And, Mr. Licina, just one last question about that topic, although we're done with that document. That was the last time you appeared in the Croatian parliament; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time I was in the Croatian Assembly was on the 24th December, I believe, 1990. I think that was the last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the next topic I'm going to have to probably look at a document, so perhaps this is a convenient time to take the break now even though it's minute early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sure many people are grateful to your way of doing things today. We'll take the break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, continuing more or less in chronological order, just one or two questions about Plitvice. You remember you testified on Monday briefly about events in Plitvice in late March of 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interfere. Are we done with this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, what you said about Plitvice - and this is at page 6417 of the transcript - is that Croatian -- "Croatian police forces made a raid in Plitvice. They were disguised as Italian tourists." And that's what you say was what started the conflict in Plitvice, that clash in particular at Plitvice; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said they made an incursion in the Plitvice area. They didn't come with their proper insignia, no. They came dressed as civilians, they changed their clothes overnight, and then clashes erupted. It's a bit of an unusual manner for them to arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the clash in Plitvice was actually because a Serb patrol entered the area. That was the real sort of spark to the fighting in Plitvice. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not correct. At the time, Plitvice was located in Korenica municipality, which was part of the SAO Krajina, which means that it was the Croatian forces who came to that area, not the Serbs. The Serbs had already been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, in March, 1991, Plitvice was part of Croatia; right? It may have been within the boundaries of what had been called the SAO Krajina, but it was part of Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, Plitvice was a part of SAO Krajina. At the time, SAO Krajina was declared on the 19th of December, 1990, and Plitvice were -- was within SAO Krajina, and SAO Krajina had declared its autonomy in that area. And, yes, they accepted that they were part of Croatia, however, they declared that only Croatian laws which did not -- which were not adverse to Serb interests were to be applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So the answer -- the short answer to my question is yes, that was part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, up until May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me ask you about another place where there was fighting, and this is Lovinac. Do you remember also talking about Lovinac in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about Lovinac, yes. But that was in September, the second part of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: There were actually at least two different attacks on Lovinac in 1991; one in August and one in September, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any attacks in August. This was not an attack, as I said in my evidence. In September, the command of the Knin Corps ordered that the barracks be freed so that the Gracac Brigade within the Knin Corps embarked on an operation to lift the siege of the barracks in Sveti Rok.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You testified about yesterday so there's no need to repeat that, but on the issue -- in the month of August, let me somehow you Exhibit 38 in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could see that on the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, this is -- this is a document dated the 6th of August, 1991, and it's from the SAO Krajina TO. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says in the heading "Serbian Autonomous Region Krajina, the TO staff of SAO Krajina." That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could scroll down. Thank you. And you'll see there in one of the -- I guess it's the second paragraph, it says: "There was an armed clash between our forces and the Ustashas in the village of Lovinac in Gracac." You see that; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In Gracac, in the village of Lovinac, an armed conflict erupted between our forces and Ustashas." That's what it says. From Gospic towards Gacice the tanks set out in order to establish a buffer zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you refer now that there was fighting in Lovinac in August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that. I'm giving evidence about the events in which I participated. I took part in the deblocking of the barracks in September. Now, as to whether there were fights earlier, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you of something that you said actually in your testimony on Monday - and this is at page 67 of Monday's transcript - when you were talking about Lovinac, and I'll read a few sentences to try and give context. You say: "... a police station was set up and we had no passage through part of our municipality. "Let me emphasise that as you go from Lovinac towards Gospic there is a line of Serb villages that also conducted a referendum in June and July concerning their joining to Gracac." And you said: "This was a completely legal referendum, and Gracac reacted positively to their referendum. And after the legal term, the legal delay, expired, those municipalities became part of Gracac." And this is another important part. It says: "However, we could not function as a single municipality because you couldn't reach one part of that municipality from another part." What you were talking about there, right, was that Lovinac was a Croat village and it divided Serb -- one Serb part of Gracac from another Serb part of Gracac. That's what you were saying. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Simply we had no access to the territory of the entire municipality. Lovinac had its elected representatives in the Gracac Municipal Assembly. It's quite a different matter that they chose not to participate. It was their decision to walk out on the first day. The door was always open for them. However, they chose not to participate in the work of the local Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Maybe you misunderstood me. When you said you couldn't reach one part of that municipality from another part, that wasn't about political stuff. You were talking about physically there was a division between parts of the municipality because of this Croatian village of Lovinac; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were four Croatian villages through which there was no passage. We always considered them integral part of the municipality. That was an integral part of Gracac municipality. We didn't divide it into Serbian part or Croatian part. All of that was Gracac municipality. I don't see things the way you're trying to portray them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, I don't dispute that you saw it all as one municipality. In fact, that was precisely the reason why Lovinac was attacked, wasn't it, to join those Serbs lands, to make the municipality one without a Croatian village obstructing communication between the Serb parts.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. As I have stated in my evidence in chief, the unblocking of the barracks was carried out. The forces which were in Lovinac presented a threat to the barracks in Sveti Rok, so what we did was to lift the siege of the barracks in Sveti Rok. We didn't do it on our own initiative, no. We followed the order of the Knin Corps. The brigade was duty-bound to carry out the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do I understand you now to say that, on orders from the JNA, you -- I'll withdraw that. Let me see if I understand your response. You said the forces which were in Lovinac presented a threat, and you say to the barracks in Sveti Rok. Which forces?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said in my evidence in chief, at the time many barracks throughout Croatia were placed under siege. We spoke about that, how the supply of water, electricity, and everything else was cut off, people were killed and so on. One of such barracks was the one in Sveti Rok.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. But why does -- why does -- if there was a blockade of the barracks in Sveti Rok, that doesn't justify the attack on Lovinac, does it? Lovinac was attacked because it was a Croatian village and you wanted to join up the entire municipality.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. We set out to lift the siege of the barracks. That's very clear. The barracks was in Sveti Rok. The forces that were there attacked the barracks, and the command of the Knin Corps ordered the Gracac Brigade to lift the siege of the barracks in Sveti Rok. I don't see what's unclear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And that, you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Might I ask a question at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Where is Sveti Rok in relation to Lovinac? Could you please answer, Mr. Licina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. If you have a map, I can show it on the map. These are four villages, one next to the other, and they lie in close proximity of each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So one would be immediately next to the other in proximity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. In proximity. Not just Lovinac but it's Lovinac, Sveti Rok, Licko Cerije, and Recica. These four villages were next to each other and they represented an area, a small area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: May I continue, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Please do continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if you can refer us to a page - I see you have an atlas - that would be more helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, if it's any assistance, Your Honour, it's page 25, and it's kind of in the top portion of square D2. You see "Sv. Rok," which is abbreviation for Sveti Rok, and then across a road Lovinac, in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I was just mentioning, in case it's confusing, that Sveti Rok appears as "Sv. Rok." It's just the abbreviation. I probably made it more confusing than it was before. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could we please, Mr. Licina, get the repetition of the fourth village, rather? We have Lovinac, Sveti Rok, Recica, and there is a fourth one, I think you mentioned, which we don't have the name of. If you could repeat it, we would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Licko Serija and Recica. Licko Serija and Recica. So when you leave from Gracac, first you reach the village of Stikada, and then Recica, Licko Serija, and then Sveti Rok to one side and Lovinac to the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome. Transcript says "Serija." It should be spelled C-e-r-i-j-e. Licko Cerije.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, I'm going to move to a different topic now, and it's something I believe you mentioned in your direct examination. You referred to this speech, you say, by Franjo Tudjman in which he said that there would have been no war if Croatia had not wanted war. Do you remember testifying about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I remember that. As far as I'm aware, that was uttered after the war had ended, either in 1995 or 1996. It could have been an interview or one of his public appearances. It was one of his well-known statements that there would have been no war had Croatia not wanted one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The Defence has referred on other occasions to a similar comment, saying it was in May, 1992, in Ban Jelacic square in Zagreb, after Croatia was recognised by the international community, I think it was. Is that the same speech or are you thinking of a different occasion?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, I think that this speech was given after the war had ended. I'm not fully sure, but I think so. It's quite a well-known speech. It must exist somewhere in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to show you -- well, actually --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment to confer with counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption, Your Honour. If we could see on the e-court, please, a document bearing the ERN R0309735.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry to do this to you. I'm always not up to speed. This document dated the 6th of August, 1991, has it been given an exhibit number or you don't want it in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's been previously marked as Exhibit 38.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is Exhibit 38. Thank you so much. Thank you very much. Then we can see the ERN number that you are raising.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I'm sorry we don't have this in B/C/S. We only have it in English. I'll have to read out the parts, Mr. Licina, and you'll have to listen to me. Now, just to begin with, this is about a speech given by Tudjman on the 24th of May, 1992, in Zagreb at a public rally. And the second page - if we could please turn to the second page there - the second paragraph. I'm going to read out this paragraph and tell me if it's the same one that you're thinking of. It says: "Some people and individuals in Croatia, and particularly in the world who were not Croatia's friends, used to say that the war was unnecessary, that we were to blame for it. I used to say, and I also can say now: Yes, the war would have been unnecessary had we given up our goal of creating the independent and sovereign State of Croatia." Now, based on what I've said so far, is this the same speech that you're thinking of, or this something different?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, the statement was verbatim as follows: "There would have been no war had Croatia not wanted one." I know that he gave a lot of speeches, but this was quite a memorable statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you -- did you see this or was this another thing that you read a quote in the newspaper? Did you see and hear President Tudjman state these words on television?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that on television, yes. Yes. It was broadcast. It was even re-broadcast many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me continue with what is said here. He continues to say: "Our proposal was to achieve the goal without war, to resolve the Yugoslavia crisis through the transformation of the federation in which nobody was happy, least of all the Croatian people, to resolve the crisis by creating a confederation of sovereign states, in which Croatia would have been sovereign, with its own army, currency, and diplomatic service. They refused to accept it. They complained that we were threatening the Serbs in Croatia, which was a lie, because we guaranteed them all rights. It became high time for us to say: Enough. Nobody will be the master in Croatia except the Croatian people themselves." And he continues in the next short paragraph: "We prepared ourselves for the realisation of our goal, if possible by peaceful means, but if not, then through war. And we won the war." Mr. Licina, does that jog your memory? Is that what you saw? Is this the speech that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I quoted the words verbatim, at least as far as they are familiar to me. As for the guarantees that he gave to the Serbs, what that boiled down to is that more than half a million of Serbs had been expelled, that a huge number of houses were burned down and destroyed, that Serbs were -- were forced to convert to Catholicism, and many other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It doesn't say any of that here; right? That's your interpretation. What it says here is, "We guarantee them all rights." That's what he says.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he said, but we can see how these rights were implemented. It is very clear how these rights of Serbs were put into practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And it's clear from this passage that I read to you that, at least in this speech, Tudjman wasn't saying that they wanted war. He said just the opposite, that they wanted to achieve their goals without war but then eventually there was a war. That's what he's saying, not that they wanted war; right? That's what he says in this speech.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You took one of his speeches for example. I don't know what it is about, but it is clear that they wanted the war. It is clear that he stated what he stated. And also, we are all familiar with the results. In our speeches we also called for peace. In my speech in the parliament I also urged for there to be a dialogue, and Croatia failed to respond to that appeal that I made on the 25th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think you've answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 881.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, I still do not believe you have addressed the question, the substantive question of Mr. Black, which was whether or not you accept that these excerpts, these portions that were read, they are the same speech or the same statement made by Franjo Tudjman that you were specifically referring to. I have not got an understanding as yet as to whether you accept that fact or whether you do not, and I want to understand clearly. Could you be so kind as to go more specifically to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on what I can see here, this is not the same speech. Perhaps a similar, but not the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And if I could just take this opportunity to show why it's a problem that we have not yet received the documents mentioned in the Defence opening. We haven't received, although and this is a perfect example, at page 6.029 of the transcript, of the Defence opening, there is a reference to a May, 1992, speech by Tudjman in the centre of Zagreb that's precisely this, which we've heard about on several occasions. We've never been given that Defence exhibit, which is presumably ready available, even though it was mentioned in the opening, and then now the date of the speech changes, apparently until after the war. So until they give us what they need to give us under the rules, we're kind of shadow boxing here, and I hope that will be resolved next Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that raises a very serious problem, because next Wednesday this witness will not be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and that's why I put this speech to him. If we can later on resolve that this is the speech that's been addressed at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I am afraid we are now not able to proceed with the proceedings unless we get these lists. I mean, unless you are prepared to bring this witness back for further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what the Defence stated in its opening statement is one thing. It's one matter. The testimony of Mr. Licina is another. I asked him if he had heard about the speech. He explained what he had heard and when. He gave a very concrete explanation about that. As far as our obligations are concerned, we have a deadline until Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic, but you must appreciate the difficulty in which now the entire trial is landing. Unless -- you have asked him and he told you what he told you about the speech. You have alleged that there is a speech made on the 24th of May, 1992, a copy of which you have not provided to the Prosecution. You now have a witness who is testifying about a speech that was made on the 24th of May, 1992. They don't have the speech, a copy, to check with this witness whether that is the speech. This is a real problem, and the only way we can resolve this problem, if we have to wait for the 23rd of August, is for you to bring this witness back for further cross-examination by the Prosecution, and that lengthens again the time available for the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, I cannot agree with you that the witness testified about the speech of the 24th of May. The Prosecutor presented a document of the 24th of May, 1992. The witness, during the examination-in-chief, talked about his knowledge in relation to 1995 or 1996. These are two different things. Also, the witness explained today that there were several speeches similar to this one. I don't see the problem at the moment with this speech of the 24th of May. In response to an explicit question by the Prosecutor, the witness explained that the speech that he was referring to is not the one that is being shown to him now with this document. That it's similar but that it's not the speech that he testified about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think you're going to have to help us here, Mr. Black. You're talking about a speech referred to in an opening that is supposed to be a speech of the 24th of May, 1992, and now you've got a speech of 24th of May, 1992, it doesn't seem to be the same as the one. Can you just sort of elucidate that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think I can -- I hope I can help explain this. This is the first time it's ever been suggested that there was more than one speech similar to this. Up until this point it's always been about this speech by Tudjman, this famous speech. As the witness says, it was famous. It was re-broadcast many times. Always one speech, one famous speech by Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And according to the Defence, when was that speech made?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In the opening they say that speech was made in May, 1992. Then the Prosecution, on the basis -- because we didn't receive any speech even though it was mentioned in the opening, then the Prosecution discloses to the Defence a speech we find from May, 1992, and now there is more than one speech, or the speech didn't happen in May, 1992. That's the problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you disclosed that speech to the Defence, what was the reaction of the Defence? Did they say, no, unfortunately, that's not the speech that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We received no response that I'm aware of. Your Honour, I'm prepared to proceed, but this is a good example of why we need those documents as soon as possible. And this particular document, this speech, if it's as famous as everybody says it is, it should be readily available. They could provide it to us tonight and we could discuss it tomorrow in court. I don't think it's something that needs to wait until next week if it's really such a well-known thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sure you can do that, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you gave us the deadline until Wednesday. This is a completely different question from the situation that we have in the courtroom right now. I just wanted to respond. Please allow me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't speak about the deadline, then, because I'm talking about the speech. And if you want to respond -- I'm trying to get you to be relevant here, Mr. Milovancevic. You are talking about deadlines. We have given you -- you were supposed to file these things on the 5th of July. You didn't. You were supposed to file them on the 14th of July. You didn't. You were supposed to file them on the 17th of July. You didn't. You filed them on the 19th and you still didn't file all of them. Why suddenly must we now stick to the 23rd of August simply because that's the date that you now say that you are given when you have been shifting dates like this? We have been accommodating you. We're trying to solve a problem here where cross-examination is in progress, documents are not ready for this current cross-examination, and we need those documents. And don't then shift me to 23rd of August. I'm trying to find a way that you can give us this speech if you have it, even if it's not translated, and then we can see how it can get translated. Now, henceforth speak relevantly and concisely to the point at issue. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the question here is the question of the speech, and this is an indisputable fact as far as the Defence is concerned. As far as the deadlines are, the Defence has been put into the situation -- because of the rhythm of the hearings, has been placed in a situation where it cannot fully meet its obligations. We are putting our utmost efforts to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, would you please speak to the issue. The rhythm of the trial is when the trial goes to trial the expectation is it goes on to trial every day unless there are circumstances that stop it. That rhythm doesn't change because somebody's not ready. Now just forget about the rhythm. Tell me whether you do have the speech, translated or not translated, that we can give to the Prosecution. I'm asking for that speech only. I'm not asking for other things that I said you must give on the 23rd of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this speech is something that I do not have in the courtroom at this moment, either translated or the original version. I didn't use that speech as an exhibit in the examination-in-chief. I didn't even present it to the witness. The Prosecutor did. It's up to the Prosecutor which documents he's going to use for the cross-examination. It's not my fault that he is using this speech when the witness is talking about a speech from 1995 and 1996. There is a substitution of topics here in this case. It's true that the Defence has not presented all the documents that it mentioned in its opening statement, so we would not be self-critical if we were to deny that, Your Honours, but we are not talking now here about the speech that we used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is precisely why there is a substitution of speeches, because they are now going on a witch hunt. They don't know what speech you are talking about in your opening statement, so they don't know what to ask this witness about. They know that there was a reference to a speech in May. One speech. They have a speech in May. One speech. You say that's not it. Your client says -- your witness says that's not it. Now they say what -- which is it? And that's why the Bench is asking you the questions that it's asking you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but then don't deny that the fault lies at the foot of the Defence for not providing all the documentation that the Defence relies upon. If you had given that, it would be easy for a 3-year-old to know that the speech that he's raising is not it. The speech that is relevant is the speech that you will have given a copy of. You haven't given a copy of that speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know if I was precise enough. During the examination of this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are imprecise every step of the way, Mr. Milovancevic. That is why we have speak in the manner in which we are speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with all due respect, I'm trying to understand whether you wish to understand me or not. I'm speaking very clearly, and I'm trying to say that I did not use that document used by the Prosecutor during the examination-in-chief of this witness. The Prosecutor can choose any document he wishes to use during the cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. Indeed. And he has chosen this speech. Why? Because Mr. Milovancevic, in his opening statement, referred to a speech of May, 1992, and because he doesn't have a copy of that speech, and he now comes across a speech of May, 1992, and he wants to check with the witness, Is this the speech that you possibly could have been referring to? That's the reason he does so. And there's a bit of logic in that, isn't there? Surely if you had given him the copy of that speech, he wouldn't have produced this one. He would have produced the one you'd given him a copy of, and the dispute would not be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand the problem. The Defence is trying to find the television broadcast of that speech -- not the transcript but the actual footage, and then we will transcribe it and translate it and present it as a transcript. We are trying to link those two things up so that we don't just have a translation of something that was allegedly said when there is actual footage of that. We were informed that there is footage of the speech, and we are now looking for it. And simply that is taking longer, so we are unable to meet the deadlines. We are on this question, though. If the Trial Chamber instructs us, then we can recall this witness, if necessary, if we cannot resolve that in any other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why didn't you give that explanation at the beginning to stop all this tempest?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was just saying what seemed relevant to me at the time that I was providing the explanation. I was just talking about things the way I understood them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then you misunderstood them and it became very imprecise. This is the first time I hear you giving me an explanation on this issue why you're not able to give the speech and why we are in the situation in which we find ourselves. That's all the explanation I was asking for, Mr. Milovancevic. I ask you once again to please listen to questions that come from the Bench and answer the questions as they are put to you without -- without trying to embellish the answer with other things that are irrelevant to the issue. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black, while we are dealing with this issue, I would like to resolve this problem. When you get a copy of the statement, will you still need this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's hard to know without seeing what it is, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to make the following order,

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You shall avail this witness if and when the Prosecution should need him for further cross-examination. Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. And I would just say it seems from what Defence counsel has stated that perhaps it's the case that they now have a transcript but they're waiting for the TV footage. We would be happy to have the transcript if they have something now. Again, in the opening, at least it appears from the transcript that he was quoting from something. So that seems to suggest that he had some kind of document that he could quote from. If that's a transcript, we would be happy to take that now, in the meantime, until we can get the video of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And we can play that thing now and it can be interpreted by interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, Your Honours. What I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me find the words of Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: It's on page 6029, line 16 and following.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's correct. And there it seems like he's quoting from something in the Defence opening, and then today, at page 80 of the transcript, he says: "The Defence is trying to find the television broadcast of that speech -- not the transcript but the actual footage, and then we'll be able to transcribe it and translate it ..." If that means that they have a transcript now, we'd be happy to have that while we wait for the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have the transcript, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have a series of documents, books, notes, statements by some people that refer to this speech. We don't have the direct transcript at this point in time. We do not have a transcript of the entire speech. We do have some things that we can give to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... play the actual thing? You see, this is the imprecision that I'm complaining about, Mr. Milovancevic. You've got to say what you mean. You've now given the impression that you do have the transcript but not the actual footage. Suddenly now you don't have this transcript. What must this Bench believe from what you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not say I had the transcript. I explained that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's go to the record and find out what you said. I just don't want to make allegations that -- you said -- Mr. Black, you said line --? Page 80, line --?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Line 12, Your Honour. That's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milovancevic, you are saying here, page 80, from line 10: "Mr. Milovancevic: Your Honour, I understand the problem. The Defence is trying to find the television broadcast of that speech -- not the transcript but the actual footage, and then we will transcribe it and translate it and present it as a transcript. We are trying to link those two things up so that we don't just have a translation of something that was allegedly said when there is actual footage of that." Now, what is this translation that you have of something that you don't have the footage of?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm just repeating once again what I already said. We have excerpts of the speech, reports in various places. We do not have a transcript of the speech. And I said that it was our goal, since we did receive information that the speech can be found, that there's video footage of the speech, we're trying to obtain the video footage, to transcribe the entire speech, and then we would present the whole thing to the other side. This is what I was talking about. I wanted to tell you one more thing. In my opening statement, I did speak about the speech, I did mention it, but I also indicated that the evidence presented by the Defence through witnesses and other ways this will be shown, but this does not have to mean the broadcast of the speech itself or the presentation of the transcript. One of the ways could be to ask the witness about it. I asked this witness whether he knew about the speech from the 24th of May. He said he didn't know anything about it but that he was aware of speeches from 1995 and 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to supply the excerpts that you say you have in the various reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received a deadline for that until the 23rd, Your Honour, and I believe that we will find that until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have received a deadline to give the full speech. I'm asking you now if you have excerpts that you say you have in various reports, Mr. Milovancevic. Can you please be logical and relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have 100.000 pages of material in the office, and we are selecting from the material some things that are important to us. It's not easy to find one's way around. I don't have the excerpts here with me because I did not think that it would be necessary to present them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the answer I want. Just tell me you don't have the excerpts. That's the simple question I was asking you, and I don't want to know about the 100.000 pages that you have in your office and the deadline of the 23rd. Please learn to stay relevant when you answer questions. I really -- my patience is running out now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I think you will agree that what is at issue here essentially is the identification of a particular speech by Franjo Tudjman and a particularly material portion of his speech. Now, I do recall that during the course of the cross-examination of the Prosecution witnesses you put the fact of this statement, this material statement, to several Prosecution witnesses, and you contextualise it in putting questions concerning the speech to various Prosecution witnesses. Did you not at that time put a date to the witnesses, and was this date a date other than the 24th of May, 1992, because maybe the record itself of your cross-examination could shed further light. I wonder if perhaps Mr. Black could assist on this, but that would throw further light in helping to identify and contextualising specifically which particular speech he's referring to, because I would think in cross-examination you would have the date as a material thing to place the speech and contextualise it. No?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. You're absolutely right. During cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses, I did present the speech of the 24th of May on Ban Jelacic square and the quotation by Tudjman that there would have been no war had Croatia not wished that. I did present that to the witnesses, and I asked them whether it was correct if they heard such a speech, and we got our answers. That would be the answer to your specific question, yes. It is not beyond -- it is beyond dispute that I did put such questions to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Milovancevic. Then I'm compelled to go on to ask you the next question: When this witness responded in cross-examination by Mr. Black, and indeed I believe in chief by you, concerning this statement of Mr. Tudjman, did you not at that time understand him to be referring to a speech made, as you had suggested to the witness in your own cross-examination of the OTP witnesses, a speech made on the 24th of May, 1992? And I believe your answer must be in the affirmative unless we're all very greatly mistaken. We're compelled to that conclusion. Would you not agree? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour. You are not wrong. You are absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the witness here whether he heard the -- about the speech on the Ban Jelacic square, and the witness said that he had heard of some later speeches. He answered that he heard the speech in 1995 or 1996. That's the problem. The problem is in the date. So I didn't press further on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So what --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What you -- what you will produce to us, then, would be the speech concerning the 24th of May, 1992, or the speech concerning what the witness is saying in 1995 or 1996? Because I think what we're faced with is a previous inconsistent statement essentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence is obliged to, and I understood it to be my task, to try to show that Mr. Tudjman spoke like that. So now we have to try to find this speech. We are going to try to find this footage so that we can present it to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What I was trying to understand from you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: -- this speech that you would be -- I'm so sorry. Thank you very much. This speech that you will be searching for, would the relevant date that you yourself are searching for, would it be in 1995 or 1996 or would it be in relation to the 24th of May, 1992? Because to me that is a very material issue at this point, in identification. Because if you are going to be searching for the speech of the 24th of May, 1992, then it would be quite different from if you were searching for the one of 1995 or 1996, as I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood His Honour Judge Moloto and my learned friend from the Prosecution that the Defence is obliged to find the speech of the 24th of May, 1992, in any case. It is in the interests of the Defence to find the other speeches too, and we think it's important that we do find those speeches and present them in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I don't think I can take it any further, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have -- I have questions arising from Judge Nosworthy's questions to you, Mr. Milovancevic. You say you asked this witness if -- if he was aware of this speech made in May, 1992, and he said, no, he's aware of speeches that were made in 1995 and 1996. Did this witness also say to you, in answer, that the speeches that he's aware of, of 1995 and 1996, in those speeches, too, Mr. Tudjman said there wouldn't have been any war if Croatia didn't want to? In other words, what I'm trying to establish is is there a possibility that these alleged words were uttered on more than one occasion? Is that how he answered you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I put one question to him on this speech and the witness answered that he heard the words that he quoted but that this was in 1995, 1996. And after that, as far as I can recall, the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did he hear these words in a speech in 1995, 1996?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, that's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So this is another speech in 1995 or 1996 that you know nothing about but that the witness may possibly know about in which the same words are alleged to have been said by the same speaker, as was said in 1992? Thank you very much. We have cleared that point. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. One -- just, no, before I proceed, there was a question from Her Honour Judge Nosworthy whether this had come up in cross-examinations, and I just point out at transcript 599 and transcript 1247. Those are two occasions. I'm not sure that was all the occasions, but it was two occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: When the 24th of May was put.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I believe May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The point that my colleague urges upon me is that he must have had a basis for cross-examining at that time, and so he must -- and he's made references to -- I don't know if it was news reports or books, but some places that say what he thinks was said in May, 1992, we don't have that yet. We don't see why we couldn't have that today or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At some stage, I'm sorry, I should have actually given Judge Hoepfel an opportunity to ask the question. He had asked -- Judge Hoepfel was asking. Mr. Milovancevic indicated that he doesn't have those excerpts here in court. Does this mean they can be brought tomorrow? And I think that's the question that Judge Hoepfel wanted to ask you, Mr. Milovancevic. Can you -- are you able to give these excerpts from which you were quoting tomorrow? Please listen to me: Excerpts. Not the speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Exactly. This is what I wanted to ask you. Several excerpts, you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, looking at the clock, we are near the end of today's proceedings. I will do my utmost to bring those excerpts tomorrow morning. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Black, would you like to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, let me turn your attention to another topic that was addressed in your direct examination, when Defence counsel was asking you questions. You talked to us about Miljevac plateau, Maslenica, and the Medak pocket; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you said, for instance, at transcript 6 and 13 of yesterday, you said that the UN failed to condemn these attacks by Croatian forces and that in a sense that "practically encouraged" the Croatians to continue with these attacks.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that mild condemnations were expressed, but Croatia did not suffer any sanctions because of that. Perhaps there was some form of criticism expressed, but no sanctions. And Croatia did not withdraw from those territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me -- let me look at one United Nations document. It's the ERN 00086197 to 6199. We'll look at three United Nations resolutions on this issue. This is the first.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there a Serbian version?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, there is not a Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I gave the wrong number, Your Honour. I'd like to look first at DK003830 to 3831. I apologise for the mistake. It's a different UN resolution. In fact it's United Nations Security Council Resolution 762 from the 30th of June, 1992. That's the one I'd like to look at, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, is it 763 or 762? In the transcript I see 762, but in my headset I just heard 763.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: 762. Thank you for the clarification. If we could scroll to the bottom of that page, please. At point number 2 there, the United Nations Security Council: "Urges all parties and others concerned to honour their commitments to effect a complete cessation of hostilities and to implement the United Nations peacekeeping plan." And then if we could turn the page, please. Paragraph 3 continues: "Also urges, in accordance with paragraph 4 of Resolution 727 (1992), the government of Croatia to withdraw its army to the positions held before the offensive of 21 June, 1992, and to cease hostile military activities within or adjacent to the United Nations Protected Areas." And then point 4 there, just briefly, it: "Urges the remaining units of the Yugoslav People's Army, the Serb Territorial Defence forces in Croatia, and others concerned to comply strictly with their obligations under the United Nations peacekeeping plan, in particular with regard to the withdrawal and the disarming of all forces in accordance with the plan."
